fatal_errors: The proposed electrochemical dealloying route does not reconstruct the reported spray-drying/thermal decomposition-reduction method.
It assumes a prealloyed bulk HEA, whereas the target method begins with homogeneously mixed aqueous salts and simultaneously forms the alloy and three-dimensional nanoframework.
It omits the essential H2 reduction at approximately 300°C and the noble-metal-seeded hydrogen dissociation mechanism that enables incorporation of Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe.
Selective removal of less noble elements conflicts with the target objective of retaining homogeneous multielement, single-phase HEA compositions.
The claim that a high-entropy composition will be retained after dealloying is unsupported and may fail through compositional depletion or phase segregation.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad goal of creating a porous three-dimensional noble-metal framework and proposes a scientifically recognizable route with a reasonably falsifiable experiment. However, it is not a reconstruction of the target work. The target uses spray drying of mixed precursor salts followed by low-temperature H2 thermal decomposition-reduction to produce self-supported HEA-3DNFs. Its key explanation is that initially reduced Pt, Ir, or Ru surfaces dissociate hydrogen and facilitate reduction and lattice incorporation of less noble metals; Pd and noble-metal-free controls do not behave similarly. The generated hypothesis instead relies on selective electrochemical dissolution from an already formed dense HEA, gives unrelated room-temperature conditions, and predicts compositional removal rather than homogeneous alloy formation. Its morphology and generic catalytic-performance predictions overlap only at a high level. The proposed controls and microscopy/electrochemistry could test the alternative hypothesis, but no evidence supports successful retention of high entropy or compositional uniformity after dealloying.
